newsitem.title: GERMANY: MMBG collapse points to shakeup of German cable TV.
newsitem.headline: MMBG collapse points to shakeup of German cable TV.

text.p: When shareholders in Germany's shattered digital television group Multimedia Betriebs GmbH (MMBG) meet on Thursday there will few pieces to pick up after Deutsche Telekom AG officially announces its withdrawal.

On the eve of a fateful meeting of MMBG's owners in Telekom's plush offices in Bonn's "government quarter," Bertelsmann AG, a key force behind MMBG, hinted strongly that it, like Telekom itself, was ready to call it quits.

"Three months of digital television have shown that it is extraordinarily difficult to find subscribers willing to pay 1,000 marks for a decoder," Bertelsmann board member Thomas Middelhoff told reporters in Berlin on Wednesday.
"We will take cautious, clear steps in this market and will not invest billions."

Middelhoff was referring to the slow take-up of arch-rival Leo Kirch's DF1, so far Germany's only digital pay TV service, which industry observers believe has no more than 3,000 subscribers. Kirch does not comment on DF1 subscriber levels.
Klaus Mangold, head of the Debis services division of Daimler-Benz AG, which is a minor shareholder in MMBG, also indicated that his company was planning to pull out.
"There are a lot of reasons for us to not maintain our shareholder status. Debis does not have a strategic interest in MMBG," he said.
Earlier this week, Deutsche Telekom pulled the carpet out from under its MMBG alliance with leading European broadcasters when it announced that it would leave the group.
MMBG was to market a common digital decoder and avoid a battle over technology standards in the new industry like the war between VHS and Betamax video recorders.

Telekom is MMBG's largest shareholder with 27 percent and plays a key role because it owns the cable TV network. Other investors include Bertelsmann, Compagnie Luxembourgeoise de Telediffusion (CLT), French pay TV group Canal Plus, TV network RTL and public broadcasters ARD and ZDF.

Telekom's move comes after it realised that Kirch's recent spending spree to amass a powerful arsenal of rights to Hollywood movies and World Cup soccer left MMBG broadcasters with little in the way of digital programming.

Telekom's decision was an aggressive move, urged by the banks preparing its November listing, to keep its cable network independent and be in a position to receive premium rates from pay TV operators like DF1 or Premiere, the analogue pay TV channel owned by Bertelsmann, Kirch and Canal Plus.
"We want to improve our cable network," said Telekom chairman Ron Sommer after a news conference on Tuesday. "One thing we aren't is a subsidy provider for our partners."
According to analysts with close ties to Telekom, the withdrawal from MMBG is just the first step in a reorganisation of how it operates its cable TV business.
"At the moment their revenue per subscriber is 162 marks a year compared to 620 marks per year on average for UK cable operators," one analyst said on condition of anonymity.

Telekom's awakening to the potential of its cable network is good news for future investors. But it could be bad news for broadcasters like Premiere and DF1, which depend on cable and satellite networks to broadcast programming to German homes.
Sommer said Telekom would soon take bids on its own digital decoder technology to allow it to market programming over the cable and share more of the revenue earned by programmers.

Industry observers expect Telekom to seek negotiations with programmers like DF1 after MMBG is officially buried and that as a result the further development of digital TV in Germany could be delayed for months or years.
